title: Bunions
metaTitle: Bunion Treatment in Kirkland, WA | Run Doctor Podiatry
metaDescription: Looking for bunion treatment Kirkland WA? Run Doctor offers gait exams, custom orthotics, and conservative care first. Call us to book a visit today.
summary: A bunion is a bony change at the joint of the big toe. It can make shoes feel tight and steps feel sore. Our podiatrists start with simple, conservative care.

quickFacts.label: Common in
quickFacts.value: Adults, often with a family history of bunions

quickFacts.label: Often felt
quickFacts.value: A sore bump on the inside of the big toe

quickFacts.label: First step
quickFacts.value: Roomy shoes, padding, and a foot exam

overview: Bunion treatment in Kirkland starts with knowing what a bunion really is. A bunion is a bony change at the joint where the big toe meets the foot. The big toe often leans toward the smaller toes, and a bump forms on the inside edge of the foot. That bump can get red, sore, or swollen, especially when it rubs on a shoe.

Many people think tight shoes cause bunions. Shoes can make the pain worse, but they are not the only cause. Foot shape, how your foot moves, loose joints, and family history all play a part. That is why two people in the same shoes can have very different feet. Bunions often change slowly, so early care may help you stay comfortable.

At Run Doctor, Dr. Lawrence Maurer and Dr. Kate Cryderman see bunions in runners, walkers, and active people from Kirkland, Totem Lake, Bellevue, and Redmond. Most people start with conservative care. Surgery is only one option, and we talk about it when other care is not enough or when the problem needs it. We explain every choice in plain words.
symptoms: A bony bump on the inside edge of the big toe joint
Pain or soreness at the base of the big toe
Red, warm, or swollen skin over the bump
The big toe leaning toward the second toe
Calluses or corns where the toes press together
Stiffness or less motion in the big toe
Shoes that feel tight or rub on the bump

causes.title: Foot shape and family history
causes.text: Bunions often run in families. You may inherit a foot shape or joint type that makes the big toe more likely to drift over time, sometimes starting in the teen years.

causes.title: How the foot moves
causes.text: The way your foot rolls and loads as you walk or run can add stress to the big toe joint. Flat feet or a low arch may increase this strain over many steps.

causes.title: Loose or flexible joints
causes.text: Some people have extra motion in the middle of the foot. This may let the first foot bone shift and the big toe lean, which can help a bunion form.

causes.title: Tight or narrow shoes
causes.text: Pointed shoes and high heels squeeze the toes and can make bunion pain worse. Shoes are not the only cause, but a roomy toe box often helps comfort.

causes.title: Arthritis or past injury
causes.text: Arthritis, an old injury to the big toe, or some nerve and muscle conditions can change the joint over time. These may add to a bunion or make it more painful.

diagnosis: Your visit starts with a talk about your pain, your shoes, your activities, and your family history. Then we look at the bump, the big toe joint, and how well the toe moves. We watch you stand and walk, and we may use gait analysis to see how your foot loads. X-rays may be used to see the bones and joint when we need more detail. This helps us tell how far the bunion has changed and which care steps make sense for you.

treatments.title: Shoe changes
treatments.text: Shoes with a wide toe box and a soft upper may reduce rubbing on the bump. We can suggest what to look for so you can shop with confidence.

treatments.title: Padding and toe spacers
treatments.text: Soft pads may cushion the bump and ease pressure from shoes. Spacers can sometimes help when the big toe presses on the second toe. We show you how to place them.

treatments.title: Custom orthotics
treatments.text: Custom orthotics cannot straighten a bunion, but they may lower strain on the big toe joint by supporting how your foot moves as you walk or run.

treatments.title: Activity changes and rest
treatments.text: Short breaks, softer surfaces, or a different mix of exercise may calm a sore joint. We help you stay active while the area settles down.

treatments.title: Anti-inflammatory care and ice
treatments.text: Ice and other measures may ease swelling after a flare. We talk with you about what is safe for your health and your needs. Rest also helps.

treatments.title: Surgery when needed
treatments.text: Surgery may be an option when pain stays high, daily life is limited, or care steps are not enough. We review the choices and what recovery may look like before you decide.

whenToSeeUs: Bunion pain most days, even in comfortable shoes
A bump that is growing or a toe that keeps drifting
Open sores, thick calluses, or skin that breaks down over the bump
A big toe joint that is red, hot, swollen, or very stiff
Trouble walking, running, or standing as long as you want
prevention: Choose shoes with a wide toe box and room for your toes to spread.
Limit time in narrow, pointed, or high-heeled shoes.
Have your foot checked if bunions run in your family.
Ask about orthotics if your arches are low or your feet roll in.
Replace worn running shoes so your foot stays well supported.

faqs.q: Is bunion treatment in Kirkland always surgery?
faqs.a: No, bunion treatment in Kirkland does not always mean surgery. Most people start with conservative care such as wider shoes, padding, custom orthotics, and activity changes. These steps may ease pain and reduce strain on the joint. Surgery is an option when pain stays high or the toe limits daily life. Your podiatrist will explain your choices first.

faqs.q: Can shoes cause bunions?
faqs.a: Shoes can make bunions hurt more, but they are not the only cause. Foot shape, loose joints, how you walk, and family history also matter. Tight or pointed shoes may rub the bump and add pain. Roomy shoes with a wide toe box often help comfort, though they may not change the bone itself.

faqs.q: Do bunions go away on their own?
faqs.a: No, a bunion usually does not go away on its own because it is a change in the bone and joint. Symptoms may ease with better shoes, padding, and orthotics. Bunions often change slowly, so early care can help you stay active. A podiatrist can check how fast yours is changing.

faqs.q: Can orthotics fix a bunion?
faqs.a: Custom orthotics cannot straighten a bunion, but they may reduce pain and strain on the big toe joint. They support how your foot moves, which can ease pressure with each step. Orthotics often work best together with good shoes and other conservative care. A gait exam helps us see if they fit your needs.

faqs.q: When should I see a podiatrist for a bunion?
faqs.a: See a podiatrist when a bunion hurts most days, rubs sores, or makes shoes hard to wear. Also book a visit if the big toe is stiff, the joint is red and swollen, or the bump is growing. Early care often gives you more options. Call 425-899-3234 to schedule a visit.

keywords: claw toe and hammer toe care
h1: Hammer Toe Treatment in Kirkland, WA
summary: A hammer toe is a toe that bends at the middle joint, often making it look curled. It can rub in shoes and cause corns. Early care may keep it more flexible.

quickFacts.label: Common in
quickFacts.value: Adults, often the second, third, or fourth toe

quickFacts.label: Often felt
quickFacts.value: Rubbing, corns, or pain on top of the bent toe

quickFacts.label: First step
quickFacts.value: Roomy shoes and a check of toe flexibility

overview: Hammer toe treatment is about easing pressure on a toe that has started to bend. In a hammer toe, the middle joint of a smaller toe curls upward, so the tip may point down. The bent joint can rub on the top of your shoe. That rubbing often leads to a corn or a sore spot, and the toe may feel tender when you walk.

A hammer toe often begins as a flexible toe. You may be able to straighten it with your hand. Over time, the joint can get stiff and stay bent. That is one reason early care matters. Muscle imbalance, foot shape, and tight shoes can all play a role, and sometimes more than one is at work. Checking the toe early gives you more choices.

At Run Doctor in Kirkland, we see hammer toes in runners, hikers, and everyday walkers from Totem Lake, Bothell, and across the Eastside. Dr. Lawrence Maurer and Dr. Kate Cryderman focus on conservative care first. Surgery may be an option if the toe is rigid, painful, or does not respond to other steps. We go over each choice with you.
symptoms: A toe that bends down at the middle joint
A corn or callus on top of the bent joint
Pain or rubbing when you wear shoes
Soreness at the tip of the toe where it presses down
Swelling or redness around the bent joint
A toe that starts flexible and slowly gets stiff
Trouble finding shoes with enough room on top

causes.title: Muscle and tendon imbalance
causes.text: When the small muscles and tendons in the foot pull unevenly, a toe can slowly bend. This may happen with certain foot types, such as high arches or flat feet.

causes.title: Tight or short shoes
causes.text: Shoes that crowd the toes can hold a toe in a bent position. Over time, the joint may adapt to that shape and stay curled.

causes.title: Other toe problems
causes.text: A bunion can push the big toe against the second toe and help it bend. Past toe injuries may also change how a toe sits and moves.

causes.title: Foot shape and family history
causes.text: Some people are born with a toe length or foot shape that makes hammer toes more likely. A long second toe, for example, may be pushed into a bend.

causes.title: Nerve or joint conditions
causes.text: Arthritis and some nerve or muscle conditions may change how the toes move. These can lead to toe deformity, so a full foot check is helpful.

diagnosis: We start by asking when the toe began to bend, where it rubs, and what shoes you wear. Then we check the toe joint to see if it is still flexible or has become stiff. We look at your arches, your other toes, and how you stand and walk. Gait analysis may show how your foot loads in motion. X-rays may be used when we need to see the bones and joints more clearly. This helps us match care to your toe.

treatments.title: Shoes with more toe room
treatments.text: A deep, roomy toe box can lower pressure on the top of the bent joint. We help you pick styles that fit your foot and your activities.

treatments.title: Padding and toe sleeves
treatments.text: Soft pads and sleeves may cushion a sore corn or the toe tip. They may ease rubbing, though they do not straighten the toe. We help you find a good fit.

treatments.title: Custom orthotics
treatments.text: Orthotics may change how your foot loads and may reduce strain that adds to toe bending. They often help most when the toe is still flexible.

treatments.title: Toe exercises and stretching
treatments.text: Gentle toe stretches and small foot muscle exercises may help a flexible toe. We show you how to do them and what to avoid. Short, steady practice works best.

treatments.title: Corn and callus care
treatments.text: We can safely trim and care for thick skin in the office. Please do not cut corns at home, since it is easy to slip or hurt the skin.

treatments.title: Surgery when needed
treatments.text: Surgery may be considered when a toe is stiff, painful, or keeps causing sores after conservative care. We explain the options and recovery before you choose.

whenToSeeUs: A toe that is bent and painful most days
A corn or sore that keeps coming back or will not heal
A bent toe that is getting stiff and cannot be straightened
Open skin, drainage, or redness near the toe, which needs prompt care
Diabetes or poor circulation with any toe change or sore
prevention: Wear shoes with a deep, roomy toe box and a good fit.
Check that your toes can wiggle freely in every pair.
Avoid long stretches in pointed or high-heeled shoes.
Treat bunions and other foot problems early.
Check your feet often for new corns or red spots.

faqs.q: What is the best hammer toe treatment?
faqs.a: The best hammer toe treatment depends on whether the toe is still flexible. For many people, roomy shoes, padding, orthotics, and toe exercises are a good start. A stiff toe may need other steps. A podiatrist can check your toe, explain what fits your foot, and tell you if surgery is worth discussing.

faqs.q: Can a hammer toe be straightened without surgery?
faqs.a: A flexible hammer toe may improve with conservative care, but results vary. Roomy shoes, padding, orthotics, and stretches may ease pain and help the toe stay mobile. A stiff, fixed toe usually does not straighten without surgery. A foot exam will show which type you have.

faqs.q: Is a hammer toe the same as a claw toe?
faqs.a: No, they are not the same, though they look alike. A hammer toe bends at the middle joint. A claw toe bends at both the middle and end joints and may curl more. Both can rub in shoes and cause corns. A podiatrist can tell which one you have.

faqs.q: Do I need hammer toe treatment in Kirkland if it does not hurt?
faqs.a: Not always, but a check is wise. A painless hammer toe can still stiffen over time, and corns may appear later. If you live in Kirkland or nearby, a visit can show if the toe is flexible. Early advice on shoes and care may save you trouble.

faqs.q: When is surgery needed for a hammer toe?
faqs.a: Surgery is only needed when a toe is rigid and painful, keeps causing sores, or does not respond to conservative care. Many people never need it. If surgery is an option, your podiatrist will explain the goal, the steps, and the recovery so you can decide with full information.

h1: Morton's Neuroma Treatment in Kirkland, WA
summary: Morton's neuroma is an irritated nerve between the toes, most often the third and fourth. It can feel like burning or a pebble in your shoe. Conservative care often helps.

quickFacts.label: Common in
quickFacts.value: Adults, especially runners and people in tight shoes

quickFacts.label: Often felt
quickFacts.value: Burning or tingling in the ball of the foot

quickFacts.label: First step
quickFacts.value: Wider shoes, cushioning, and a foot exam

overview: Morton's neuroma treatment begins with learning what is happening in the ball of your foot. A nerve runs between the long bones of the forefoot. When that nerve gets squeezed or irritated, it can thicken and become sore. Most often this happens between the third and fourth toes. Many people say it feels like they are stepping on a pebble or a bunched-up sock.

The pain may come and go. It can flare during a run, in a tight shoe, or after standing for a long time. You may feel burning, tingling, or numbness that spreads into the toes. Taking off your shoe and rubbing the area often brings some relief. Neuroma symptoms can look like other forefoot problems, so a proper exam is useful.

At Run Doctor, Dr. Lawrence Maurer and Dr. Kate Cryderman see forefoot nerve pain in runners, hikers, and busy workers from Kirkland, Redmond, Woodinville, and Seattle. We look at your shoes, your foot motion, and your activity. Care starts with conservative steps. Surgery may be an option if pain stays strong after other care. We explain each step clearly. Ask us anything.
symptoms: Burning pain in the ball of the foot
A feeling of a pebble or fold of fabric under the toes
Tingling or numbness in the toes next to each other
Pain that gets worse in tight or narrow shoes
Sharp or shooting pain during walking or running
Relief when you take off your shoe and rub the foot
Pain that may come and go over weeks or months

causes.title: Pressure on the forefoot nerve
causes.text: A nerve between the toe bones can be squeezed with each step. Over time, the nerve may become irritated and thick, which can cause burning or tingling.

causes.title: Tight or narrow shoes
causes.text: Shoes that squeeze the front of the foot, including high heels, can press the toe bones together. This may add pressure on the nerve and make symptoms flare.

causes.title: High-impact sports
causes.text: Running and other sports that load the ball of the foot may add stress to the nerve. Hard surfaces and worn shoes can add to that load.

causes.title: Foot shape and motion
causes.text: Flat feet, high arches, or a foot that rolls a lot can change pressure in the forefoot. Gait and biomechanical checks often show why the nerve is irritated.

causes.title: Other toe or foot problems
causes.text: Bunions, hammer toes, and past injuries can change how weight moves across the forefoot. This may increase pressure near the nerve.

diagnosis: We ask where the pain is, what it feels like, and which shoes or activities set it off. During the exam, we gently press between the toes and squeeze the forefoot to look for the nerve pain and a clicking feeling. We check your toes, arches, and how you walk. Gait analysis may show where pressure builds. Ultrasound or X-rays may be used to help rule out other causes, such as stress injuries or joint problems.

treatments.title: Shoe changes
treatments.text: Shoes with a wide toe box and good forefoot cushioning may take pressure off the nerve. We can help you pick styles for work, running, and daily life.

treatments.title: Padding and metatarsal support
treatments.text: A small pad placed just behind the ball of the foot may spread the toe bones and reduce nerve pressure. We show you where it should sit.

treatments.title: Custom orthotics
treatments.text: Custom orthotics can change how your foot loads and may ease pressure on the forefoot nerve. They are often a key part of care for runners.

treatments.title: Activity changes
treatments.text: Cutting back on high-impact work for a time, or changing surfaces and shoes, may help calm the nerve. We help you plan a smart return to training.

treatments.title: Injection options
treatments.text: For some people, an injection near the nerve may be discussed to help calm pain and swelling. We review the benefits, limits, and risks first.

treatments.title: Surgery when needed
treatments.text: Surgery may be considered when pain stays strong after conservative care. We explain what it involves, what recovery may look like, and other options before you decide.

whenToSeeUs: Burning or tingling in the ball of the foot that lasts more than a few weeks
Pain that keeps you from running, walking, or working as you like
Numb toes that do not clear up after you change shoes
Pain that wakes you at night or gets worse over time
Diabetes or nerve problems with any new foot numbness
prevention: Wear shoes with a roomy toe box, especially for long days on your feet.
Replace worn running shoes before they lose cushioning.
Limit high heels and very narrow styles.
Build running mileage slowly rather than all at once.
Ask for a gait check if forefoot pain keeps coming back.

faqs.q: What is the best Morton's neuroma treatment?
faqs.a: The best Morton's neuroma treatment often starts with simple steps. Wider shoes, forefoot padding, custom orthotics, and less impact activity may ease nerve pressure. Many people improve with conservative care. If pain stays strong, a podiatrist can talk about injections or surgery. A foot exam helps choose the right plan for you.

faqs.q: How do I know if I have a neuroma or something else?
faqs.a: Only an exam can tell for sure, since several problems cause forefoot pain. A neuroma often feels like burning, tingling, or a pebble under the toes, and it may flare in tight shoes. Stress injuries, joint problems, and arthritis can feel similar. A podiatrist can check and order imaging if needed.

faqs.q: Can running cause a neuroma?
faqs.a: Running may add stress to the forefoot nerve, but it is rarely the only cause. Tight shoes, foot shape, and how your foot moves also matter. Many runners in Kirkland and nearby improve by changing shoes, adding padding, and using orthotics. A gait exam can show why your forefoot is overloaded.

faqs.q: Does a neuroma go away on its own?
faqs.a: A neuroma may calm down when the pressure is reduced, but it does not always go away alone. Wider shoes, padding, and orthotics often help symptoms. If you keep wearing tight shoes or doing the same load, it can linger. A podiatrist can help you find a plan that fits your routine.

faqs.q: When is surgery needed for Morton's neuroma?
faqs.a: Surgery is only considered when pain stays strong after conservative care. Many people do not need it. If it comes up, your podiatrist will explain what the procedure involves, the possible risks, and what recovery may look like. You will have time to ask questions and decide what feels right.

metaTitle: Ingrown Toenail Treatment in Kirkland, WA | Run Doctor

h1: Ingrown Toenail Treatment in Kirkland, WA
summary: An ingrown toenail happens when the edge of a nail presses into the skin. It can cause pain, redness, and swelling. Careful in-office care may ease it and lower the chance of infection.

quickFacts.label: Common in
quickFacts.value: Teens, adults, athletes, and people with curved nails

quickFacts.label: Often felt
quickFacts.value: Tender, red, swollen skin along the nail edge

quickFacts.label: First step
quickFacts.value: Gentle foot soaks and a safe nail check

overview: Ingrown toenail treatment in Kirkland often begins with a simple question: is the skin only sore, or is it infected? An ingrown toenail happens when the side of a nail grows into or presses against the skin next to it. The big toe is most often affected. The skin can turn red, swollen, and very tender, even from a light touch or a sock.

Several things can lead to it. Cutting nails too short or rounding the corners is common. Tight shoes, toe injuries, sweaty feet, and naturally curved nails can also play a part. Runners and soccer players may get them from repeated pressure on the toes. Ingrown nails can affect kids, teens, and adults. Knowing the cause helps prevent a repeat. It is a small habit.

Dr. Lawrence Maurer and Dr. Kate Cryderman see ingrown nails at Run Doctor for people from Kirkland, Totem Lake, Bothell, and Bellevue. We treat children and adults. Please do not cut or dig at the nail edge at home, since this can make things worse. If you have diabetes, poor circulation, or signs of infection, call us soon for prompt care.
symptoms: Pain along the side of a toenail, often the big toe
Redness and swelling next to the nail edge
Skin that feels warm or tender to the touch
Pain when wearing shoes or socks, or when the toe bumps something
Clear fluid or pus near the nail, which may signal infection
Skin that grows over the edge of the nail
A nail that looks curved or thick at the sides

causes.title: Cutting nails too short
causes.text: Cutting nails very short or curving the corners can let the edge grow into the skin. Trimming straight across usually helps keep the nail edge above the skin.

causes.title: Tight or poorly fitting shoes
causes.text: Shoes that squeeze the toes press the nail edge into the skin. Shoes that are too short can also jam the toes with every step.

causes.title: Toe injury or repeated pressure
causes.text: Stubbing a toe, dropping something on it, or running and kicking can change how a nail grows. Repeated small hits may also irritate the nail fold.

causes.title: Curved or thick nails
causes.text: Some people have naturally curved nails, and this may run in families. Thick nails from fungus or past injury can also press on the skin.

causes.title: Sweaty feet and poor nail care
causes.text: Damp skin can become soft and easier to irritate. Picking at nails or tearing the edge may leave a sharp spur that grows into the skin.

diagnosis: We ask when the pain began, how you trim your nails, and whether you have diabetes, poor circulation, or past infections. Then we look at the toe, the nail edge, and the skin around it. We check for signs of infection, such as warmth, swelling, drainage, or red streaks. We also look at your shoes and how your toes fit in them. In most cases, this exam lets us decide on the safest treatment for that nail.

treatments.title: Safe home care for mild cases
treatments.text: For mild soreness, soaking the foot in warm water and keeping the toe clean and dry may help. Wear roomy shoes. Do not cut or dig at the nail edge.

treatments.title: Careful nail edge care in the office
treatments.text: We can gently lift or trim the nail edge that is pressing on the skin. This is done with the right tools and in a clean setting.

treatments.title: Partial nail removal
treatments.text: If the nail keeps growing in, we may remove the side that is causing the problem after numbing the toe. This often eases pain right away.

treatments.title: Treating infection
treatments.text: If the toe is infected, we may clean the area and talk about next steps, which can include medicine. Prompt care matters, especially with diabetes.

treatments.title: Stopping regrowth of the problem edge
treatments.text: For nails that keep coming back, a procedure on the nail root may be an option. It aims to keep that nail edge from growing back in.

treatments.title: Help with shoes and nail trimming
treatments.text: We show you a safe way to trim nails and how to choose shoes that give your toes room. This may help lower the chance of a repeat.

whenToSeeUs: Increasing pain, redness, swelling, or warmth around the toenail
Pus, drainage, or a bad smell from the toe
Red streaks or a fever, which need urgent attention
Diabetes, poor circulation, or numb feet with any ingrown nail
An ingrown nail that keeps coming back
prevention: Trim nails straight across and do not round the corners.
Leave a little white edge on the nail instead of cutting it very short.
Wear shoes with enough room for your toes.
Protect your toes during sports with well-fitting shoes.
Keep feet clean and dry, and change damp socks.

faqs.q: How do I treat an ingrown toenail at home?
faqs.a: For mild soreness, soak your foot in warm water, dry it well, and wear roomy shoes. Do not cut, dig, or tear at the nail edge, since that can push the nail deeper or cause infection. If the toe is not better in a few days, or looks infected, see a podiatrist.

faqs.q: When is an ingrown toenail an emergency?
faqs.a: Seek prompt care if you see spreading redness, red streaks, pus, fever, or fast-growing swelling. Anyone with diabetes, poor circulation, or numb feet should call right away, even for mild symptoms. These conditions make infections harder to fight. Call our office at 425-899-3234, or get urgent care if you feel very unwell.

faqs.q: Is ingrown toenail treatment in Kirkland painful?
faqs.a: We aim to keep you as comfortable as possible. For procedures, we numb the toe first, so most people feel pressure rather than sharp pain. The toe may be sore after the numbing wears off. We explain what to expect, how to care for the toe, and when to check in.

faqs.q: Can an ingrown toenail go away on its own?
faqs.a: A very mild ingrown nail may settle on its own with soaks, roomy shoes, and time. But many keep growing into the skin and become more painful or infected. If it does not improve within a few days, a podiatrist can help. Early care is often simpler and quicker.

faqs.q: Do kids get ingrown toenails?
faqs.a: Yes, children and teens can get ingrown toenails, often from tight shoes, sports, or nail trimming that is too short. Kids should not dig at the nail either. A podiatrist can treat them gently. Dr. Cryderman treats all ages, so families from Kirkland and nearby can bring children in too.

metaTitle: Athlete's Foot Treatment in Kirkland, WA | Run Doctor Care
metaDescription: Itchy, peeling feet? Learn about athlete's foot treatment and when to see a podiatrist. Run Doctor serves Kirkland and the Eastside. Call to book a visit.
h1: Athlete's Foot Treatment in Kirkland, WA
summary: Athlete's foot is a fungal skin infection that often starts between the toes. It can cause itching, peeling, and redness. Most cases may be eased with proper care, but stubborn ones should be checked.

quickFacts.label: Common in
quickFacts.value: Active people, swimmers, and those in damp shoes

quickFacts.label: Often felt
quickFacts.value: Itching, burning, and peeling skin between the toes

quickFacts.label: First step
quickFacts.value: Keep feet dry and see us if it lingers

overview: Athlete's foot treatment starts with knowing the cause. Athlete's foot is a fungal skin infection of the feet. The fungus likes warm, damp places, so it often starts between the toes. It can cause itching, burning, and red, peeling, or cracked skin. In some people it spreads to the soles or sides of the feet, where the skin may turn dry and scaly.

You can pick up the fungus from damp floors in locker rooms, pools, and showers. Sweaty socks and shoes that stay wet can help it grow. Many people have mild symptoms and brush them off. But the skin may crack, and the fungus can spread to other areas or to the toenails. That is why lasting itching should be taken seriously.

At Run Doctor, Dr. Lawrence Maurer and Dr. Kate Cryderman see athlete's foot in runners, swimmers, gym-goers, and busy families from Kirkland, Redmond, Woodinville, and Seattle. We confirm what the rash is, since other skin problems can look the same. Persistent cases or nail changes should be evaluated, and we help you choose a plan that fits your health. You will get clear advice.
symptoms: Itching or burning between the toes
Peeling, flaky, or cracked skin
Red or scaly skin on the soles or sides of the feet
Small blisters that may ooze or crust
A bad smell from damp, soft skin
Thick, yellow, or crumbly toenails that may mean the fungus has spread
A rash that keeps coming back after treatment

causes.title: Damp, warm feet
causes.text: Fungus grows well in moist skin. Sweaty feet, wet socks, and shoes that do not dry out can make it easier for an infection to start.

causes.title: Shared wet spaces
causes.text: Locker rooms, pool decks, and shared showers can carry fungus. Walking barefoot in these places may expose your feet to it.

causes.title: Tight or non-breathing shoes
causes.text: Shoes that trap heat and sweat help fungus thrive. Closed shoes worn for long hours, such as boots or sports shoes, can add to the problem.

causes.title: Small breaks in the skin
causes.text: Cracks, blisters, or small cuts can let fungus in more easily. Dry, cracked heels and skin between the toes are common spots.

causes.title: Health factors
causes.text: Diabetes, a weak immune system, or poor circulation can make foot infections more likely or harder to clear. These conditions need prompt, careful care.

diagnosis: We ask how long the rash has been there, where it itches, what you have tried, and whether you have diabetes or other health issues. Then we look at the skin between and under your toes, your soles, and your toenails. Other conditions, such as eczema, dry skin, or allergic rash, can look like athlete's foot. When needed, we may take a small skin or nail sample to check for fungus. This helps us choose the right treatment.

treatments.title: Keeping feet clean and dry
treatments.text: Wash your feet daily and dry well between the toes. Change damp socks often. A dry environment makes it harder for the fungus to grow.

treatments.title: Antifungal products
treatments.text: Antifungal creams, sprays, or powders may help clear many mild cases when used as directed. Please follow the label, and ask us if you are unsure.

treatments.title: Prescription treatment
treatments.text: If the rash is stubborn, widespread, or comes back, a prescription antifungal may be needed. We pick the right option for you and talk about safety.

treatments.title: Caring for shoes and socks
treatments.text: Fungus can stay in shoes. Letting shoes dry fully, rotating pairs, and washing socks in hot water may lower the chance of a repeat. Fresh socks each day also help.

treatments.title: Treating cracks and infection
treatments.text: Cracked skin can let bacteria in. We check for infection and talk about how to care for open skin so it can heal properly. Early care matters.

treatments.title: Checking the nails
treatments.text: If the toenails look thick or yellow, the fungus may have spread there. Nail fungus is slower to clear, so we review the options with you.

whenToSeeUs: Itching or peeling that lasts more than a couple of weeks of home care
A rash that keeps coming back
Thick, yellow, or crumbly toenails
Swelling, warmth, pus, red streaks, or increasing pain, which may mean infection
Diabetes or poor circulation with any foot rash or crack in the skin
prevention: Dry your feet fully, especially between the toes, after bathing or swimming.
Wear sandals or shower shoes in locker rooms and pool areas.
Choose breathable socks and change them when they get damp.
Let your shoes dry out between wears, and rotate pairs.
Do not share towels, shoes, or nail tools.

faqs.q: What is the best athlete's foot treatment?
faqs.a: For mild athlete's foot, an over-the-counter antifungal cream or spray used as directed, along with keeping feet dry, often helps. Stubborn or widespread cases may need prescription care. Because other rashes look similar, a podiatrist can confirm the cause. Please see us if there is no change after a couple of weeks.

faqs.q: Is athlete's foot contagious?
faqs.a: Yes, athlete's foot can spread to other people and to other parts of your body. The fungus can live on damp floors, towels, and shoes. You can lower the risk by wearing shower shoes, keeping feet dry, and not sharing towels or footwear. Treating it early also helps limit spread.

faqs.q: How do I know if it is athlete's foot or something else?
faqs.a: You cannot always tell by looking, since eczema, dry skin, and allergic rashes can look the same. Athlete's foot often itches and peels between the toes. If a rash does not improve or keeps coming back, a podiatrist can check it and test for fungus if needed.

faqs.q: Should I see a podiatrist in Kirkland for athlete's foot?
faqs.a: See a podiatrist in Kirkland if home care does not help, the rash returns, your nails look thick or yellow, or you have diabetes or poor circulation. Signs like swelling, pus, or red streaks need prompt care. We can confirm the cause and choose a safe plan. Call 425-899-3234.

faqs.q: Can athlete's foot spread to my toenails?
faqs.a: Yes, the same fungus can spread to the toenails. Nails may turn thick, yellow, or crumbly. Nail fungus is harder to treat than skin fungus and often needs longer care. If you notice nail changes with athlete's foot, have them evaluated so the right treatment can start sooner.
